title: The Web: HTML, CSS and JavaScript
description: How a page reaches the browser, how HTML and CSS shape it, and how JavaScript brings it to life, read closely enough to predict what the code does before you run it.
audience: A capable adult who uses the web every day and has seen some code. They know what a variable and a loop are from cs-basics, and need no previous HTML, CSS or JavaScript.
outcomes: You'll be able to trace a URL to the tree the browser builds.
You'll be able to predict which CSS rule wins and how wide an element will be.
You'll be able to predict what JavaScript prints, including coercion, closures and event-loop order.
You'll be able to read fetch, storage and event code and spot the usual bugs and injection risks.

modules.title: Documents and style
modules.summary: How a page reaches the browser, how HTML gives it structure, and how CSS decides what every element looks like and where it sits.

modules.title: JavaScript, the language
modules.summary: Values, coercion, functions, scope, objects and the event loop, read and traced without a runner.

modules.title: The page comes alive
modules.summary: The DOM, events, talking to servers, storing data in the browser, and keeping pages accessible and fast.

lessons.title: What the browser receives
lessons.objective: Trace a URL through DNS, an HTTP request and response, and the parser to a tree of nodes, and read the parts of a URL and the family of a status code.

concepts.title: Parts of a URL
concepts.summary: A URL names a scheme, a host, an optional port, a path, a query and a fragment, and the browser never sends the fragment to the server.

concepts.title: Request and response
concepts.summary: The browser sends a method, a path and headers, and the server replies with a status code, headers and a body.

concepts.title: Status code families
concepts.summary: The first digit tells the story: 2 means success, 3 redirection, 4 a fault in the request and 5 a fault in the server.

concepts.title: The DOM tree
concepts.summary: The parser turns the HTML text into a tree of nodes, repairing malformed markup by fixed rules instead of failing.

misconceptions: Learners think the browser shows the HTML file as written. In fact it shows a tree built from the file, so two files that look different can build the same tree.
Learners think a 404 or 500 means the network failed. The server answered perfectly well; the status code is the answer.
Learners think the whole URL is sent to the server. The fragment after # stays in the browser, which is why it can drive in-page jumps without a request.
sequence: Open with typing https://shop.example.com:8443/items/42?color=red&size=m#reviews and ask what travels where.
Break the URL into scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment, and say which pieces form the request line and Host header.
Show one request and one response as plain text, naming the method, status line and a content-type header.
Group status codes by first digit, then name the handful learners meet: 200, 201, 301, 304, 400, 401, 403, 404, 500.
Show the bytes becoming a tree: the parser repairs a missing closing tag, and the tree, not the text, is what CSS and JavaScript later use.
examples: URL https://shop.example.com:8443/items/42?color=red&size=m#reviews: host shop.example.com, port 8443, path /items/42, query color=red&size=m, fragment reviews.

Markup

One

Two has no closing tags, and the parser builds two p elements (checked in a DOM implementation).

A table written as
x
gains a tbody element in the tree, so the table's first child is TBODY, not TR.

figures.learnerAction: Switch between the four views and hover a URL part to see which message carries it.

lessons.title: Structure and meaning
lessons.objective: Choose the HTML element that says what content is rather than how it looks, and predict what a screen reader can navigate by.

concepts.title: Semantic element
concepts.summary: An element whose name states its role, such as nav, main, button or h2, so that software can use the page without seeing it.

concepts.title: Accessible name
concepts.summary: The text that assistive technology announces for a control, taken from its label, content or alt text.

concepts.title: Heading outline
concepts.summary: Headings h1 to h6 form an outline that readers and screen readers jump through, so levels should follow the content's real nesting.

concepts.title: Label and control
concepts.summary: A label tied to its input by for and id makes the label text part of the control's name and enlarges the click target.

misconceptions: Learners think headings are for sizing text. Size is CSS's job; a heading's level states where the text sits in the outline.
Learners build buttons from div elements with click handlers. A div has no keyboard focus, no role and no Enter or Space activation unless each is added by hand.
Learners treat alt text as a caption. It replaces the image for someone who cannot see it, and decorative images take an empty alt so they are skipped.
sequence: Show one page built entirely from div elements and the same page built from header, nav, main, article and footer, and ask what a screen reader can list in each.
Walk through links versus buttons: a link goes somewhere, a button does something.
Show an input with and without a label, and read out the accessible name each produces.
End with images: informative alt, decorative empty alt, and why 'image of' is noise.
examples: A news page uses h1 for the site name, h3 for each story and h2 for the sections; a heading-jump listing shows levels 1, 3, 3, 2, 3, which skips level 2 under the first story.
<input id=email> next to the text Email with no label element has no accessible name beyond its placeholder; <label for=email>Email</label> gives it the name Email.
inside a link that also contains the text 'Home' is correct, because the link's name comes from the text.

figures.shows: The same small page twice: a div soup with grey boxes, and a landmark layout labelled banner, navigation, main, contentinfo. A third view shows the list of landmarks a screen reader exposes.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle the two markups and the screen-reader view.

figures.shows: Four small snippets, one per task (site menu, delete action, page title, product photo), each with candidate elements.
figures.learnerAction: Pick the element for each snippet.

questionPlan.sample: Which element is correct for a control that deletes the selected row on click?
Which HTML5 element marks the block of primary navigation links?
An is purely decorative, a flourish between paragraphs. Which alt is correct?

lessons.title: The box and the flow
lessons.objective: Compute the width and height an element occupies from content, padding, border and margin, and predict how block and inline boxes flow and how vertical margins collapse.

concepts.title: Box model
concepts.summary: Every element is a rectangle of content surrounded by padding, then border, then margin.

concepts.title: box-sizing
concepts.summary: With content-box the declared width covers only the content; with border-box it covers content, padding and border.

concepts.title: Normal flow
concepts.summary: Block boxes stack vertically and inline boxes fill lines, until a layout mode changes that.

concepts.title: Margin collapse
concepts.summary: Adjoining vertical margins between block siblings combine into the larger of the two, not the sum.

misconceptions: Learners add margin to width as if it were part of the element's size. Margin sits outside the border and is never clickable background.
Learners believe width: 200px always means a 200px-wide element. Under content-box the border box is wider; under border-box it is exactly 200px.
Learners expect margins between stacked blocks to add. 30px under 20px yields a 30px gap.
sequence: Draw a div: width 200px, padding 10px 20px, border 5px, margin 15px, and compute each box edge.
Rewrite the same div under border-box and watch the content shrink.
Stack two paragraphs with margin-bottom 30px and margin-top 20px and measure the gap.
Say which layout modes (flex, grid, floats) do not collapse margins, as a pointer to the next lesson.
examples: Content-box: width 200, padding 20 left and right, border 5 each side gives a border box of 200+40+10 = 250px wide and a margin box of 250+30 = 280px.
Border-box: the same declared width of 200px makes the content 200-40-10 = 150px wide.
Sibling margins 30px and 20px collapse to a 30px gap, not 50px.

figures.shows: A box-model diagram with a draggable content width and sliders for padding, border and margin; edges are labelled with their computed pixel sizes. Views: content-box, border-box.
figures.learnerAction: Change the numbers and watch the total width; switch box-sizing.

figures.shows: Two stacked paragraphs with their margins shaded and a ruler beside the gap.
figures.learnerAction: Change each margin and read the gap.

questionPlan.sample: An element has width: 200px, padding: 10px 20px, border: 5px solid and box-sizing: content-box. What is the width in px of its border box?
With box-sizing: border-box, width: 200px, padding: 10px 20px and border: 5px solid, what is the content width in px?
Paragraph A has margin-bottom: 30px and the paragraph below it, B, has margin-top: 20px. Both are normal block siblings. What is the gap in px?

lessons.title: Which rule wins
lessons.objective: Rank competing CSS declarations by origin, importance, specificity and order, and say which values are inherited.

concepts.title: Specificity
concepts.summary: A selector's weight is a triple of counts: ids, then classes, attributes and pseudo-classes, then element names and pseudo-elements, compared left to right.

concepts.title: Cascade order
concepts.summary: When specificity ties, the declaration that comes later wins, and !important or inline styles change the ranking.

concepts.title: Inheritance
concepts.summary: Some properties, such as colour and font-family, pass to children unless overridden, while others, such as border and margin, do not.

concepts.title: Custom properties
concepts.summary: A --name value is inherited and read with var(), so one change can restyle many rules.

misconceptions: Learners think the rule written last always wins. Order only breaks ties after specificity.
Learners think ten classes beat one id. The columns are compared left to right, not added, so one id outranks any number of classes.
Learners expect border to inherit like colour. Only some properties inherit.
sequence: Score #nav .item a:hover step by step.
Compare .btn.primary against div .btn and decide the winner.
Show :where() adding zero and :is() taking its highest argument.
Inheritance: set color on body and watch which descendants follow and why a link still ignores it by default.
Close with the habit: keep specificity low and flat, and avoid !important.
examples: #nav .item a:hover scores (1,2,1): one id, two classes or pseudo-classes (.item and :hover), one element.
.card:hover > p::first-line scores (0,2,2): .card and :hover, then p and ::first-line.
.btn.primary is (0,2,0) and div .btn is (0,1,1), so .btn.primary wins whatever the order.

figures.shows: A specificity calculator pre-filled with other selectors (not those in the questions): each selector in its own row, columns for ids, classes and elements, and a rank column.
figures.learnerAction: Type a selector and read the triple; sort the rows to see the winner.

figures.shows: A small DOM tree with a colour set on the root and arrows showing which nodes inherit and which stop.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle properties between inherited and non-inherited.

questionPlan.sample: Give the specificity of .card:hover > p::first-line as three comma-separated counts (ids,classes,elements).
Rule 1 is .btn.primary { color: red } and appears first. Rule 2 is div .btn { color: blue } and appears later. A div contains <a class='btn primary'>. What colour is the link text?
choices: it depends on the order of the class names

questionPlan.sample: body { color: green; border: 1px solid; } and a paragraph inside body. Which is true of the paragraph?
questionPlan.answer: Its text is green but it has no border.
choices: Its text is green but it has no border.
It has a border and green text.
It has a border but black text.

lessons.title: Layout with flexbox and grid
lessons.objective: Predict item sizes in a flex row from basis, grow and shrink, and in a grid from fr units, gaps and fixed tracks.

concepts.title: Flex main axis
concepts.summary: A flex container lays its items along one axis and distributes free space or overflow between them by grow and shrink factors.

concepts.title: Grow and shrink
concepts.summary: Free space is split in proportion to flex-grow and overflow is removed in proportion to flex-shrink times basis.

concepts.title: Grid tracks
concepts.summary: A grid defines rows and columns, and fr units share the space left after fixed tracks and gaps.

concepts.title: Flexbox or grid
concepts.summary: Flexbox arranges one dimension of content-sized items, while grid places items in two dimensions against a track plan.

misconceptions: Learners think flex-grow sets a width. It splits only the leftover space, after each item's basis.
Learners think 1fr means an equal share of the whole container. It is a share of what remains after fixed tracks and gaps.
Learners use grid for every row of buttons or flex for every page frame. Each tool has a natural dimension.
sequence: Start with a 600px row and three 100px items, then let them grow 1, 2 and 3.
Overflow: three 150px items in a 300px row shrink equally.
Grid: 800px wide, columns 1fr 2fr 100px, gap 20px, and where the remaining space goes.
A decision rule: one row or column of items that wrap, use flex; a page frame or card board with rows and columns, use grid.
examples: Container 600px, flex-basis 100px for all three items, flex-grow 1, 2 and 3: free space 300px splits 50 per unit, so widths are 150, 200 and 250px.
Container 300px, three items with basis 150px and flex-shrink 1: overflow 150px, each loses 50px, final widths 100px each.
Grid 800px, columns 1fr 2fr 100px, column-gap 20px: 800-40-100 = 660px for fr tracks, so columns are 220, 440 and 100px.

figures.shows: A flex row and a grid, each with draggable container width and numeric inputs for grow, shrink, fr and gap. Item widths are read off as labelled rulers. Views: flex, grid.
figures.learnerAction: Change the container width and the factors, and read each item's width before answering.

figures.shows: Four layouts (nav bar, photo wall, page frame, tag list) with a choice of flex or grid.
figures.learnerAction: Match each layout to its best tool.

questionPlan.sample: A 600px flex row has three items with flex-basis 100px and flex-grow 1, 2 and 3. How wide in px is the third item?
A grid is 800px wide with grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 100px and column-gap: 20px. How wide in px is the 2fr column?
A 300px flex row holds three items with flex-basis 150px, flex-shrink 1 and no minimum widths. How wide in px does each end up?

lessons.title: Responsive design
lessons.objective: Convert rem, em, percent and viewport units to pixels, and decide which media query rules apply at a given viewport width.

concepts.title: Relative units
concepts.summary: rem scales from the root font size, em from the element's own or parent's font size, and vw from the viewport width.

concepts.title: Media query
concepts.summary: A media query applies its rules only while its condition, such as min-width, is true for the current viewport.

concepts.title: Mobile first
concepts.summary: Base rules serve the narrowest screen, and min-width queries add complexity as space allows.

concepts.title: Viewport meta
concepts.summary: Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers lay the page out at a wide virtual width and shrink it to fit.

misconceptions: Learners think em always means the root size. It is relative to the font size of the element or its parent, so nesting compounds.
Learners think a media query tests the device. It tests the viewport or other features at that moment.
Learners write max-width queries last and fight their own cascade; mobile first keeps rules additive.
sequence: Root font size 16px: 1.25rem is 20px; a parent at 20px with a child of 1.5em gives 30px and a grandchild 45px.
A viewport of 700px against @media (min-width: 768px) and (max-width: 1024px).
5vw on a 1200px viewport is 60px.
Show why one column on a phone and three on a laptop need no JavaScript.
examples: 1.25rem at a 16px root is 20px.
A parent with font-size 20px, its child at 1.5em is 30px, and its child again at 1.5em is 45px.
On a 700px-wide viewport, @media (min-width: 768px) is false, so the wide-screen rules do not apply.

figures.shows: A viewport ruler from 320 to 1440px with breakpoint markers at 768 and 1024, and a page thumbnail that reflows to one, two or three columns as a handle moves.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the handle to a width and read which media blocks are active.

questionPlan.sample: The root font size is 16px. What is 1.25rem in px?
A parent has font-size: 20px. Its child has font-size: 1.5em and the grandchild also font-size: 1.5em. What is the grandchild's size in px?
The viewport is 700px wide. Which rule block applies? A) @media (min-width: 768px) B) @media (max-width: 767px) C) @media (min-width: 600px) and (max-width: 800px)

lessons.title: Values, types and coercion
lessons.objective: Predict the result of an expression that mixes strings, numbers, booleans, null, undefined and arrays, using the language's conversion rules rather than guesses.

concepts.title: Primitive types
concepts.summary: JavaScript has seven primitive types (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol) and everything else is an object.

concepts.title: Coercion
concepts.summary: Operators convert operands to the type they need: + concatenates if either side is a string, while - * and / convert both sides to numbers.

concepts.title: Strict versus loose equality
concepts.summary: === compares type and value with no conversion, while == converts before comparing, with null == undefined as a special case.

concepts.title: Floating-point numbers
concepts.summary: Numbers are 64-bit floating point, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 and integers are exact only up to 2^53 - 1.

misconceptions: Learners think typeof null is 'null'. It is 'object', a historical quirk that remains for compatibility.
Learners think + adds. If either operand is a string it concatenates, so '5' + 3 is '53', yet '5' - 3 is 2.
Learners reach for == because it 'works'. [] == false is true and null == 0 is false, so == hides bugs that === exposes.
sequence: Evaluate '5' + 3 and '5' - 3 side by side, and say why the operators differ.
Number('') is 0 and Number('12px') is NaN, and parseInt('12px') is 12; compare conversion strictness.
Show 0.1 + 0.2 and the largest safe integer 9007199254740991.
Truthiness: the falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined and NaN; '0' and [] are truthy.
Close with a rule of thumb: use === and !==, convert explicitly, and use ?? when 0 or '' are valid values.
examples: '5' + 3 is '53'; '5' - 3 is 2; '3' * '4' is 12; true + true is 2 (all checked in Node 22).
null == undefined is true, null == 0 is false, null >= 0 is true, NaN === NaN is false, and [] == false is true.
[10, 9, 1].sort() is [1, 10, 9] because the default sort compares strings.

figures.shows: A grid of expressions (rows, using operands different from the questions) against operators (+, -, ==, ===) with result cells hidden until chosen, showing the conversion applied.
figures.learnerAction: Predict each cell, then reveal it and the conversion step that produced it.

figures.learnerAction: Step through and name the type at each stage.

questionPlan.sample: What does console.log('5' + 3, '5' - 3) print?
What does typeof null evaluate to? Give the string.
What does console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3) print?
What does console.log([10, 9, 1].sort()) print?

historyNotes: Brendan Eich wrote the first version of JavaScript in about ten days in May 1995 at Netscape; the typeof null result comes from that first implementation. Confirm wording before using.

lessons.title: Functions, scope and closures
lessons.objective: Trace which variable a name refers to across function, block and closure scopes, including hoisting and the var-in-loop trap.

concepts.title: Lexical scope
concepts.summary: A name is resolved by looking outward from where the code was written, not where it is called.

concepts.title: Hoisting and the temporal dead zone
concepts.summary: A function declaration is usable before its line, a var is declared early but undefined until assigned, and let or const throw until their line runs.

concepts.title: Closure
concepts.summary: A function keeps access to the variables of the scope it was created in, even after that scope has returned.

concepts.title: Per-iteration binding
concepts.summary: A let in a for loop head creates a fresh binding each iteration, while var shares one across the loop.

misconceptions: Learners think a closure copies the variable's value. It keeps the variable itself, so later changes are visible.
Learners expect var in a loop to capture each iteration's value, and get the final value every time.
Learners think all declarations behave the same before their line. Function declarations work, var gives undefined and let throws a ReferenceError.
sequence: Make a counter: a function that returns a function and keeps n alive.
Create two counters and show their states are independent.
Run the same loop of three timers with var and then let.
Print typeof f and typeof g for a function declaration and a var holding a function expression, before their lines run.
examples: function makeCounter(){ let n = 0; return () => ++n; } with a and b made separately; calling a() twice, b() once, then logging a() and b() prints 3 2.
for (var i=0;i<3;i++) setTimeout(()=>console.log(i),0) prints 3 3 3, and with let prints 0 1 2.
console.log(typeof f, typeof g) before function f(){} and var g = function(){} prints function undefined.

figures.shows: A program with a makeAdder(step) function and two adders made with different steps, stepping through calls and showing each closure's private variables as boxes that live on after makeAdder returns (a different program from the questions).
figures.learnerAction: Step and read both counters' n.

figures.shows: Nested scope rings (global, function, block) with a name lookup arrow moving outward. Views: var, let.
figures.learnerAction: Pick a name and watch where the lookup stops.

questionPlan.sample:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
What is printed, in order?

lessons.title: Objects, arrays and references
lessons.objective: Predict when two names share one object, what a spread copy does and does not copy, and what array methods return or mutate.

concepts.title: References
concepts.summary: Assigning an object or array copies the reference, so two names then point at one object.

concepts.title: Shallow copy
concepts.summary: Spread and Object.assign copy the top level only, so nested objects stay shared.

concepts.title: map, filter and reduce
concepts.summary: map returns a new array of the same length, filter a subset, and reduce folds the array into one value.

concepts.title: Mutating methods
concepts.summary: push, splice and sort change the array in place, while slice, map, filter and toSorted return new ones.

misconceptions: Learners think const makes the object immutable. It fixes the binding, and the object can still change.
Learners think {...o} makes an independent copy. Nested objects are still shared.
Learners think sort returns a sorted copy. It sorts in place and returns the same array.
sequence: const a = [1,2,3]; const b = a; b.push(4) and the length of a.
A nested object copied with spread, a nested change, and the original.
['1','2','3'].map(parseInt) and why the index becomes the radix.
structuredClone for deep copies.
examples: a = [1,2,3]; b = a; b.push(4) leaves a.length equal to 4.
o = {x:{y:1}}; c = {...o}; c.x.y = 2 leaves o.x.y equal to 2; structuredClone(o) would not share x.
[1,2,3,4].map(n=>n*2) is [2,4,6,8], filter(n=>n>4) is [6,8], reduce sum is 14.
['1','2','3'].map(parseInt) is [1, NaN, NaN].

figures.shows: Two names drawn as arrows to one array box holding strings, and a second view with a spread copy sharing an inner object, using different values from the questions.
figures.learnerAction: Step through each statement and watch the arrows.

figures.shows: A three-stage pipeline view of a different array, [5,6,7], mapped, filtered and reduced.
figures.learnerAction: Step through the stages.

questionPlan.sample:
console.log([1,2,3,4].map(n => n * 2).filter(n => n > 4).reduce((s, n) => s + n, 0));
What is printed?

lessons.title: The event loop and promises
lessons.objective: Predict the order in which synchronous code, promise callbacks, await continuations and timers run.

concepts.title: Call stack
concepts.summary: JavaScript runs one piece of synchronous code to completion before anything else runs.

concepts.title: Task and microtask queues
concepts.summary: After the stack empties, all queued microtasks (promise callbacks) run before the next timer or I/O task.

concepts.title: Promise states
concepts.summary: A promise is pending, then fulfilled or rejected exactly once, and then callbacks are queued as microtasks.

concepts.title: await
concepts.summary: await pauses the async function and resumes it as a microtask when the awaited promise settles.

misconceptions: Learners think setTimeout(fn, 0) runs immediately. It queues a task that runs only after the stack and all microtasks finish.
Learners think await blocks the program. It suspends only the async function, and other code runs meanwhile.
Learners think a promise callback runs when the promise resolves. It is queued, and runs when the current code finishes.
sequence: Print 1, set a zero-delay timer, queue a promise callback, print 4, and ask the order.
Rewrite with an async function that awaits null.
Add a microtask queued from inside another microtask to show that the queue drains fully.
Show the loop as a picture: stack, microtask queue, task queue.
examples: console.log(1); setTimeout(()=>console.log(2),0); Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log(3)); console.log(4) prints 1, 4, 3, 2.
console.log('c'); f(); console.log('d') with async function f(){ console.log('a'); await null; console.log('b') } prints c, a, d, b.
A promise callback that queues another promise callback runs both before the next timer (checked in Node 22).

figures.shows: The event loop: call stack, microtask queue and task queue as three lanes, with a step button that moves each queued function. Views: a promise example and an await example built from different statements than the questions (two then callbacks and a timer).
figures.learnerAction: Step the loop and watch what runs when.

figures.shows: Five console.log calls from a mixed program to be sorted into execution order.
figures.learnerAction: Drag into order before running the stepper.

questionPlan.answer: c a d b (one per line)

questionPlan.sample: Why does a setTimeout callback with a delay of 0 run after a promise callback queued later?
questionPlan.answer: Promise callbacks are microtasks and run before the next timer task.
choices: Promise callbacks are microtasks and run before the next timer task.
Zero is treated as a delay of one second.
Promises always run before any other code.
The timer was cancelled by the promise.

lessons.title: The DOM and events
lessons.objective: Select and change nodes, and predict the order and target of events as they capture down and bubble up through nested elements.

concepts.title: DOM API
concepts.summary: The document is a tree of nodes with methods to find, create, change and remove them.

concepts.title: Elements versus nodes
concepts.summary: childNodes includes text and comment nodes, while children includes only elements.

concepts.title: Bubbling and capture
concepts.summary: An event travels down to its target and then back up, firing listeners on each ancestor, with capture listeners on the way down.

concepts.title: Event delegation
concepts.summary: One listener on a parent can handle events from many children, using event.target to find which one.

misconceptions: Learners think children and childNodes match. Whitespace between tags makes text nodes, so a ul with two li elements has five child nodes.
Learners think a click only reaches the element they clicked. It bubbles, so listeners on ancestors fire as well.
Learners think stopPropagation cancels the default action. It only stops travel; preventDefault cancels the default.
sequence: Parse a three-line ul and count children and childNodes.

lessons.title: Talking to servers
lessons.objective: Read fetch code and predict what happens on a 404, a network failure and a repeated body read, and write and read JSON correctly.

concepts.title: fetch promise
concepts.summary: fetch resolves with a Response for any HTTP status and rejects only when the request itself fails.

concepts.title: response.ok
concepts.summary: ok is true for status 200 to 299, and code must check it before trusting the body.

concepts.title: JSON
concepts.summary: JSON is text with double-quoted keys and strings, and stringify drops undefined, functions and symbols from objects.

concepts.title: Same-origin policy
concepts.summary: A page can read responses only from its own origin (scheme, host and port) unless the server opts in with CORS headers.

misconceptions: Learners think fetch rejects on 404. It resolves, and response.ok is false.
Learners think JSON.stringify keeps everything. undefined and functions vanish from objects and become null in arrays, and NaN becomes null.
Learners think CORS is a server-side security wall. It is a browser rule that decides whether page code may read a cross-origin response.
sequence: Sketch the request lifecycle with fetch, await, ok check, json().
Run the same fetch against 200, 404 and an unreachable host and state what each does.
Stringify an object with undefined, a function, NaN and a Date.
Compare origins: http versus https, port 443 versus default, subdomains.
examples: fetch of a 404 URL resolves with ok false and status 404 (checked against a local server).
JSON.stringify({a:undefined,b:()=>1,c:NaN,d:new Date(0)}) is {"c":null,"d":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"}; JSON.stringify([undefined, function(){}]) is [null,null].
https://a.com and https://a.com:443 share an origin; http://a.com and https://a.com do not; https://b.a.com and https://a.com do not.

figures.shows: A flowchart of a fetch call with branches for network failure (rejects), non-2xx (resolves, ok false) and success, each ending in a code box.
figures.learnerAction: Pick a scenario and follow the path.

figures.learnerAction: Mark each pair same or different.

lessons.title: Storing state and trusting input
lessons.objective: Choose cookies, localStorage or sessionStorage for a job, predict what storage returns, and explain why textContent is safe where innerHTML is not.

concepts.title: Web storage
concepts.summary: localStorage and sessionStorage keep string key-value pairs in the browser, the first until cleared and the second until the tab closes.

concepts.title: Cookies
concepts.summary: Cookies are sent to the server on matching requests, so they carry sessions, and flags such as HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite restrict how they travel.

concepts.title: Cross-site scripting
concepts.summary: If untrusted text is parsed as HTML, an attacker's script runs with the page's authority.

concepts.title: Safe sinks
concepts.summary: textContent inserts text as text, while innerHTML parses markup and so must never receive untrusted input.

misconceptions: Learners think localStorage keeps numbers and objects. It stores strings, so setItem('n', 5) returns '5' and setItem of an object stores '[object Object]'.
Learners store session tokens in localStorage because it is easy. Any script on the page can read it, whereas an HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by script.
Learners escape input by hand. The robust move is to avoid the parser, with textContent, and to let frameworks escape by default.
sequence: Store 5 and read it back with typeof, then add 1 to the result.
Compare localStorage, sessionStorage and cookie on lifetime, who can read them and whether the server sees them.
Insert the text hi with textContent and innerHTML and compare the DOM.
Name Content-Security-Policy as the second line of defence.
examples: localStorage.setItem('n', 5) then typeof localStorage.getItem('n') is 'string', and getItem('n') + 1 is '51'; a missing key returns null.
localStorage.setItem('o', {a:1}) stores '[object Object]'; use JSON.stringify and JSON.parse.
x.textContent = 'hi' leaves zero child elements and shows the tags as text; x.innerHTML = 'hi' creates one b element.

lessons.title: Accessible and fast
lessons.objective: Compute whether a colour pair meets the contrast minimum, and name what each Core Web Vital measures and its good threshold.

concepts.title: Contrast ratio
concepts.summary: Contrast is (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05) from the lighter and darker relative luminances, from 1:1 to 21:1, and WCAG AA asks for 4.5:1 for normal text.

concepts.title: Keyboard access
concepts.summary: Everything operable by mouse must be reachable and usable by keyboard, in a logical focus order, with a visible focus indicator.

concepts.title: Core Web Vitals
concepts.summary: Largest Contentful Paint measures loading, Interaction to Next Paint measures responsiveness and Cumulative Layout Shift measures visual stability.

concepts.title: What slows a page
concepts.summary: Bytes, blocking scripts and styles, and late-discovered images delay first paint, and fixes include compression, defer and explicit image dimensions.

misconceptions: Learners judge contrast by eye. A grey that looks fine on a bright monitor can fall below 4.5:1, so measure it.
Learners think accessibility is a final audit. Most of it is free if semantics, labels and focus are right from the start.
Learners think speed means total load time. The vitals measure what the user sees and feels, such as when the biggest element appears.
sequence: Black on white is 21:1, #767676 on white is 4.54:1 and passes, #777777 is 4.48:1 and fails (computed from the WCAG formula).
Tab through a page and notice a missing focus ring.
Match LCP, INP and CLS to what they measure and their good thresholds.
A banner that loads late and pushes text down: reserve its height.
examples: Contrast of #767676 on #ffffff is 4.54:1, which passes AA for normal text; #777777 gives 4.48:1, which fails; #595959 gives 7.00:1.
The good thresholds measured at the 75th percentile of page loads are LCP 2.5 seconds or less, INP 200 milliseconds or less and CLS 0.1 or less.
An image without width and height attributes loads and shoves content down, raising CLS.

courseCheck: A mixed check of: URL parts and status families; semantic element choice; box-model and flex/grid arithmetic; specificity scoring; unit conversion; coercion and equality results; closure and loop tracing; aliasing and array pipelines; event-loop ordering; event bubbling order; fetch and JSON outcomes; storage values and safe sinks; contrast arithmetic. Each item is a number, a choice, or the printed output of a short snippet.
platformNeeds: A sandboxed JavaScript runner (a worker with no network and a time limit) with code-run-javascript questions that compare console output. Until then every JavaScript question is code-reading.
A figure type for the event loop (stack, microtask queue, task queue with a step button); an svg_figure with switchable views is the fallback and is described per lesson.
A DOM/CSS sandbox figure (live HTML and CSS panel with a locked-down iframe) so the box-model, flexbox, grid and specificity lessons can be explored with real rendering instead of drawn diagrams.
A program_trace that accepts JavaScript, not only Python, for closure and aliasing lessons.
unverified: MDN pages were read from the mdn/content repository on GitHub because developer.mozilla.org was not reachable from the research sandbox; the public URLs are derived from the repository paths.

WHATWG HTML, ECMAScript, WCAG and web.dev could not be opened from the sandbox (marked verified false). The WCAG contrast formula and the Core Web Vitals thresholds (LCP 2.5 s, INP 200 ms, CLS 0.1 at the 75th percentile) are from memory.
History notes (Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989, Eich's ten days in May 1995) are from memory.
The licence of the WHATWG HTML text (CC BY 4.0) should be confirmed before any text is adapted.

All JavaScript outputs were evaluated in Node 22 (and DOM behaviour in jsdom); the DOM event order was checked in jsdom, not in a browser, though the spec ordering is the same. CSS arithmetic was computed by hand and not rendered.
